articles.title: Sen. Slotkin Says Trump “Started Another War In The Middle East, Got Us Stuck” And Is Now “Forced To Buy Russian Oil From Putin,” Claiming The Two Leaders “Share The Same Hubris” In “Failing And Expensive Wars” - NewsBreak: Local News & Alerts
articles.summary: Sen. Slotkin Says Trump “Started Another War In The Middle East, Got Us Stuck” And Is Now “Forced To Buy Russian Oil From Putin,” Claiming The Two Leaders “Share The Same Hubris” In “Failing And Expensive Wars”  NewsBreak: Local News & Alerts
articles.full_text:
By Rob Glenn,
2 days ago
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), a former CIA officer and member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, accused President Donald Trump on Tuesday of leading the United States into a stalled war in the Middle East and then turning to Russia for fuel, a move she said aids Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine. Slotkin made the remarks in a post on X at 9:38 a.m. on October 13, 2026. They came four days after the administration announced a diesel arrangement with Moscow and temporarily eased sanctions to enable it.
Slotkin’s full post reads:
“It’s hard to believe that President Trump started another war in the Middle East, got us stuck, and now is forced to buy Russian oil from Putin, aiding and abetting the war Putin started in Ukraine, in which he’s now stuck.
Trump has always weirdly admired Putin, and now they share the same hubris that got them into failing and expensive wars.”
Slotkin attached a CNBC report on the arrangement to her post. Trump announced Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under a deal he reached with Putin during a phone call. In a Truth Social post, Trump laid out the schedule: more than 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately after that. Moscow would then deliver another 3 million tons, depending on the condition of Russia’s refineries.
The Treasury License
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License No. 135 on October 9, signed by Director Bradley T. Smith. It authorizes all transactions otherwise prohibited under the Russian Harmful Foreign Activities Sanctions Regulations and the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations that relate to the “sale, delivery, offloading, or importation, including importation into the United States, of diesel fuel of Russian Federation origin.” The authorization runs through 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on April 7, 2027.
The license carves out one exception. It does not authorize any debit to an account on the books of a U.S. financial institution of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, the National Wealth Fund of the Russian Federation, or the Ministry of Finance.
The waiver temporarily lifts sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine. Those sanctions were imposed on Russian oil companies in October 2025. The report said the diesel exports could provide Russia with billions of dollars in revenue. Diesel prices fell after the announcement, but analysts said the deal may not be enough to keep them down. Diesel prices are up 70 percent since the United States and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28, and the average U.S. price reached $6.28 a gallon on Thursday, according to AAA.
Zelenskyy’s Response
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the deal immediately and warned that easing sanctions without a Russian commitment to de-escalate would only prolong the war. In a social media post, Zelenskyy said:
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
Political Pressure Over Fuel Prices
The deal comes as Trump faces growing pressure to lower fuel costs before the November midterm elections. Republicans are facing competitive races in conservative strongholds such as Iowa, where farmers are feeling the pinch of high diesel prices. The president has few options, given the destruction of global refining capacity by the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East. Trump considered a diesel export ban last month but relented after the oil industry and big business warned it would raise gasoline prices. This week he signed an executive order letting truckers use tax-exempt off-road diesel on highways without federal penalties, though the order only defers the tax obligation, which has created confusion over whether truckers may have to pay later.
The pressure is not limited to Democrats. Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers has said the Iran war “needs to end, and quickly,” arguing that higher diesel prices are driving up broader consumer costs. Iowa Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson has called for a temporary halt to diesel exports.
Slotkin’s Record on the Iran War
Slotkin’s post follows months of public statements on the conflict. On February 28, the day the United States and Israel began major military action against Iran, she released a statement saying President Trump “hasn’t made his case to the American people.” She added that he “hasn’t laid out the goals or the imminent threat posed by Iran that justifies risking a wider regional war,” and that he “hasn’t followed the Constitution and brought this issue before Congress before committing our nation to war.” She also noted her own background: “As a former CIA officer who served three tours in Iraq, I have no love lost for the Iranian government.”
On March 19, Slotkin announced she had voted in favor of the bipartisan War Powers Resolution led by Sen. Tim Kaine (D-VA), which would require any U.S. participation in hostilities against Iran to be explicitly authorized by Congress. “I voted again to support a war powers resolution that would stop President Trump’s war of choice in Iran,” she said. She cited “13 U.S. servicemembers dead and hundreds more injured, huge cost hikes on things like gas and fertilizer, and a cycle of military escalation that has no end in sight.”
In April, Slotkin responded to a message from Trump threatening military escalation in Iran. “The President of the United States is taking his threats against the Iranian people to new extremes,” she said. She added that “targeting civilians en masse would be a clear violation of the law of armed conflict as laid out in the Geneva Conventions, as well as the Pentagon’s Law of War Manual.” The release was edited after its initial publication, so the live version should be checked for final wording.
Her concerns about a drawn-out conflict predate the current war. After the June 2025 U.S. strikes on Iran, she said: “As someone who served in Iraq and saw up close the loss of blood and treasure over 20 years, I don’t want to be embroiled in another drawn out conflict, and neither do the American people.” A week earlier, after Israel’s operation against Iran, she described Iran as “a state sponsor of terror” but warned of “a spiral of violence that leads to real consequences for the U.S.”
Slotkin’s Record on Russia and Ukraine
On Russia, Slotkin joined a bipartisan coalition of 50 senators in April 2025 in introducing legislation for primary and secondary sanctions against Russia and actors supporting its aggression in Ukraine. The bill included a 500 percent tariff on imported goods from countries that buy Russian oil, gas, uranium and other products. “We need just, lasting peace for Ukraine – and that requires pressure on Russia not Ukraine,” Slotkin said then. “Enough with the games – let’s use every tool we can to secure Ukraine’s freedom and end this war.” She also noted that Michigan has a large Ukrainian population.
Earlier Sanctions Waivers
Friday’s license is not the first time the administration has eased Russian energy sanctions during the Iran war. In March, Treasury issued a 30-day waiver allowing purchases of Russian oil at sea. Administration officials defended it at the time as a way to calm markets. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the waiver could help “tamp the price spikes.” On March 8, Trump wrote on Truth Social that short-term oil prices “will drop rapidly when the destruction of the Iran nuclear threat is over” and are “a very small price to pay for U.S.A., and World, Safety and Peace.” The administration also waived sanctions on Iranian oil at sea on March 20, a step that drew criticism from lawmakers of both parties.
What It Means
Slotkin’s post links the two wars that have driven global fuel disruptions: the Iran conflict that began February 28 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Her argument is that the first has pushed the administration to ease pressure on Moscow, undermining the second. The administration has framed the waivers as a way to calm fuel markets. Zelenskyy and other critics say the revenue will help fund Russia’s war.
With midterms weeks away and diesel above $6 a gallon, the question of how to lower fuel costs without strengthening Russia is likely to stay central in Washington. General License 135 is set to run until April 7, 2027, and analysts have said the deal may not deliver lasting relief at the pump.

articles.full_text:
Russia-Ukraine War Latest News: Three killed in drone strike on Ukraine’s western city
Three people have been killed, and 12 are injured after a Russian drone attack on Ukraine’s western city of Lutsk today.
Roman Romaniuk, acting head of the Volyn regional military administration, said on Telegram that the attack involved a jet-powered Shahed drone.
The latest reports highlight the continuing threat posed by Russia’s drones, which Ukraine has found increasingly harder to intercept.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly warned of the risks to civilians and infrastructure as attacks extend beyond frontline areas and as Russia focuses on Ukraine’s energy facilities ahead of the winter.
Russia-Ukraine War Latest News: SpaceX limits Starlink operations in Ukraine – leading to ‘disruption of missions’
SpaceX has introduced a limit on some Starlink services in Ukraine, officials have said.
Ukraine’s presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said SpaceX had stopped the operation of its military-grade version above 100 miles per hour and that units had been forced to cancel some missions.
“Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions,” he wrote on Telegram.
It is not clear why Starlink has made this move.
For context: The satellite internet terminals from Elon Musk’s company are vital for guiding Ukraine’s longer-range drone strikes in occupied southern and eastern Ukraine and help the Ukrainian army with battlefield communications.
Such a move is therefore sure to disrupt combat drone missions for which the technology is crucial.
It also comes as Washington pressures Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Russia-Ukraine War Latest News: Drone fragments found on Polish beach ‘likely from military test’
Further to our post earlier on a possible drone being found on a Baltic Sea beach, we are now receiving more information.
A Polish defence ministry spokesperson says the preliminary findings indicate the fragments belong to a test drone from a Polish military aviation technology institute.
In recent years, a series of airspace incursions by Russian drones in the region have fuelled concerns about the war in Ukraine spilling over the alliance’s borders.
But, in this case, it appears to have been a false alarm.
Russia-Ukraine War Latest News: Meloni: US-Russia deal ‘very risky choice’
Donald Trump entered a controversial deal with Vladimir Putin last weekend when he struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia.
The US president said Moscow will provide “the American and global marketplace” with nearly five million US tons of diesel after a phone call with the Russian leader.
“That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you,” Trump said.
Today, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has hit out at the deal, describing it as a “very risky choice” that runs counter to efforts to force Putin to sit at the negotiating table with Ukraine.
“The outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear,” Meloni told the Italian parliament.
“It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions,” she added.
Russia-Ukraine War Latest News: Autumn attack by Russia ‘likely to fail’, analyst says – after Moscow forced to face ‘unthinkable’
“Russia’s summer offensive has failed.”
That’s the opinion of the Institute for the Study of War thinktank’s Nataliya Bugayova, who argues that Ukraine has “regained the operational initiative” in most key areas of the battlefield – with Russia’s planned autumn offensive “likely to fail as well”.
Ukraine has slowed Russian advances across the frontline this year – and made the human cost Moscow’s military has to pay even higher, Bugayova’s assessment for the US-based think tank says.
“Ukraine has retaken significant territory from Russia in 2026, and at the theatre level has nearly zeroed out Russian gains for the year,” Bugayova adds.
“ISW has observed evidence to assess that Russian forces have only made a net gain of about 100 square kilometres thus far in 2026 thanks to Ukrainian counteroffensives, which have liberated at least 1,046 square kilometres, for example.”
She adds Ukraine’s deep strike campaign has “forced the Kremlin to confront dilemmas” inside Russia that would have been “unthinkable” not so long ago.
“Ukrainian advances and strikes are challenging Putin’s promises of Russia’s economic stability, security, and greatness.”

articles.title: ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
NATO’s top general has unveiled a new war plan for countering a Russian attack on members of the alliance, embedding lessons learned from the front lines in Ukraine.
Speaking about NATO’s so-called “theory of victory” at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, General Alexus Grynkewich, who has served as head of United States European Command and the Supreme Allied Commander Europe since 2025, said the plan rests on three strategies designed to stop an invasion in its tracks: “block, blunt and break”.
Recommended Stories
The announcement comes amid mounting warnings from European intelligence agencies of rising threats from Russia, including both the prospect of conventional military action and “hybrid warfare”, which can include tactics from cyberattacks to tampering with undersea cables.
In a bid to ease the alliance’s growing concerns, Grynkewich said: “What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it.”
But the new plan from NATO comes at a time when the alliance itself appears divided on how to deal with Russia, following a series of recent overtures from US President Donald Trump to Russian President Vladimir Putin, including his latest controversial plan for Russia to release stocks of diesel to global markets despite sanctions on Russian oil.
So, what’s in the new NATO plan, and what are European agencies warning about? How has Russia reacted? And is the alliance even on the same page on all of this?
What’s in the new NATO plan?
General Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO does not view a military confrontation with Russia as “imminent or inevitable”, but that it will nevertheless be ready for one.
“Implementing the theory of victory I’ve described today would require me to issue orders that I hope to never give,” he said. “But let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”
The “block, blunt and break” strategy, he explained, is aimed at stopping an attack rather than taking enemy territory.
Drawing directly on lessons learned on the front lines in Ukraine and from conflict in the Middle East, Grynkewich said the plan relies on the use of precision weapons with “affordable mass”, like drones, and other autonomous systems.
In the plan, he said, the alliance’s forces would “block” an attack at the border to halt enemy advances on the battlefield, then “blunt” the attack by hitting incoming troops from the air, sea, and land. Then, at last, they would aim to “break” the enemy by targeting the supply chain and command networks.
“If required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” he said. “Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed.”
Are Russian threats in Europe on the rise?
Germany’s foreign intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, warned last week that the country risked being drawn into a “violent conflict” with Russia, saying Moscow increasingly viewed Berlin as a principal adversary.
He cited an attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport in August as an example of the escalating threat. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has also warned of a Russian-linked “shadow war” involving sabotage, cyberattacks and other covert operations.
In France, President Emmanuel Macron warned last month that the Russian hybrid threat facing France and other European countries had intensified in recent weeks, and ordered the preparation of plans to protect critical infrastructure.
The United Kingdom’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that he had received confirmation upon entering office that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum, although he did not publicly detail the evidence behind that assessment. Last week, he travelled to Berlin to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in part to discuss plans to combat Russian hybrid warfare.
Russia issued a nuclear warning to NATO late last month, saying it was prepared to use its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania.
In July, Romania’s Defence Ministry said it had recorded 33 instances of Russian drones entering its airspace since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Eighteen of those incursions had occurred this year, and Romanian F-16 fighter jets had shot down three drones during the year.
Poland has also accused Russian intelligence services of orchestrating an arson attack on a Starlink satellite-internet station in Wola Krobowska last month. Warsaw described the incident as part of Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against countries supporting Ukraine.
Norway, too, has issued similar warnings. Beate Gangas, head of the country’s Police Security Service, said this week that Europe is facing its most serious security situation since World War II, echoing concerns over suspected Russian sabotage and covert operations across the continent.
What has Russia said?
In August, Russia warned the UK that it could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement on August 17. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
Despite this, Russia is not preparing for “any kind” of conflict with Europe, President Vladimir Putin said last month. He added that Russia had “no real motive” to escalate tensions and criticised European countries that have suggested otherwise.
“Many in Europe talk about expecting an attack from Russia and therefore believe they must themselves prepare for hostilities, for a war with Russia,” Putin told reporters in St Petersburg.
“I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe,” he noted.
Putin added that Russia was considering its stance on whether to resume peace talks with Ukraine following recent Ukrainian attacks on Russia, particularly on energy infrastructure.
“On proposals to resume negotiations, yes, they are all on the table, and it is all possible. But after everything they’ve done, we will give careful thought to what steps we need to take in response,” Putin said.
Is NATO united?
Since taking presidential office in the US, Trump has repeatedly attacked other NATO members for not shouldering enough of the financial burden for defence. He has also been angered by NATO members’ general refusal to join in the US-Israel war on Iran.
As a result, there are fears that Trump cannot be relied on to provide support if it is needed within the NATO alliance, analysts say.
In August, after the Russian consulate in London warned of “consequences” for the UK for providing Ukraine with long-range drones, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC that could include the possibility of attacks. He said many of the military experts currently advising the Kremlin are “convinced” that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said.
The alliance is facing a deepening divide over Russia, as Trump pursues engagement with Moscow while European governments insist that Russia must remain under pressure if the war in Ukraine is to come to an end.
Last month, Washington invited Putin to December’s Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami, in a move that was seen as potentially ending Moscow’s diplomatic isolation since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The European Union responded that Russia remained a G20 member but said it would continue condemning the invasion regardless of whether Putin attended.
The divide deepened last week when Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel exports into US and global markets, temporarily easing sanctions on Russian fuel. His administration said the move could help lower energy prices and encourage Putin to return to peace negotiations.
Critics have warned that it would generate revenue for Russia while undermining Western efforts to constrain its war effort.
Meanwhile, Trump has also escalated his criticism of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and suggested that Ukraine should elect a new leader willing to make a deal with Russia. Zelenskyy had called Trump’s diesel agreement with Putin “not fair and not honest”, arguing it would benefit Russia.
EU foreign ministers also insisted that European sanctions against Russia would remain in place despite Washington’s deal with Moscow.
On Sunday, Trump claimed in a Truth Social post to have instigated an “energy truce” between Russia and Ukraine, under which both sides would refrain from targeting each other’s energy facilities with long-range strikes. However, Zelenskyy said such a deal was “news to me” – although he also said Ukraine would respect such a truce if Moscow honoured it as well. Regardless, Russia, which also has not confirmed agreeing to an energy truce, continued striking Ukraine’s facilities on Monday, according to Ukrainian officials.

Confucius Institutes, Luban Workshops connect China and Central Asia through language and skills
At the Confucius Institute of Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies, Uzbekistan, students gathered on Sept 24 to make mooncakes, a traditional Chinese delicacy, deepening their understanding of the Mid-Autumn Festival through hands-on cultural exchange.
The event is one example of how China and Central Asian countries have deepened ties in recent years through people-to-people and vocational cooperation.
Confucius Institutes have become important platforms for Central Asian students to learn Chinese, while Luban Workshops train highly skilled technical professionals to contribute to these countries' development and construction.
READ MORE: More in region are seeking to learn Chinese
Central Asia now hosts 13 Confucius Institutes, with Kazakhstan accounting for five institutes, Kyrgyzstan four, and Uzbekistan and Tajikistan two each, according to Xinhua.
At the Luban Workshop of L. N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University in Astana, Kazakhstan, robotic arms, computer workstations and drone training equipment fill a smart laboratory where students learn how computer vision supports industrial automation.
For 20-year-old student Zhansaya Abdurakhman, the workshop offers a glimpse into a future career as Kazakhstan places a growing emphasis on AI development during its Year of Artificial Intelligence.
"We studied computer vision and how to work with a robotic manipulator for industrial automation," she said. "These skills are in great demand, and such practical experience can help us prepare for jobs in modern industrial enterprises."
Kazakh Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek, who attended the university's 30th anniversary celebrations and the workshop's open day in late May, said the Luban Workshop model has proven successful in Kazakhstan.
He expressed appreciation to the Chinese government for providing industrial-grade equipment and supporting technology transfer. He said Kazakhstan is set to host three Luban Workshops, calling them a reflection of closer ties.
Ramazan Sadvokasov, a lecturer who trained in Tianjin, northern China, said the laboratory is an important platform to prepare professionals who may later help develop AI in Kazakhstan.
Nearly 100 teachers and more than 30 students have already received hands-on technical training through the program, he said.
"We expect our future graduates to become specialists in artificial intelligence, industrial automation and drone technologies," Sadvokasov said.
In Bishkek, the Luban Workshop at Kyrgyz State Technical University, or KSTU, officially opened in October 2024, with laboratories and classrooms spanning more than 1,000 square meters and housing over 300 pieces of equipment.
Akylbek Chymyrov, vice-rector of KSTU and director of the workshop, called it both an operational platform and a "living bridge" for advancing educational cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and China.
"The establishment of the Luban Workshop is of strategic importance for our university and provides a strong impetus for its modernization," Chymyrov said, adding that thanks to the substantial support of Chinese partners, KSTU students and faculty have gained access to advanced teaching methods, educational programs and high-tech equipment.
ALSO READ: Exchanges of young people contribute to friendship
Chymyrov noted that the country urgently needs modern engineers for large-scale energy and infrastructure projects, and that the workshop is training specialists with international experience and high professional standards. The workshop is equipped with 15 laboratories, three smart classrooms and a conference hall.
The two-track approach — language and culture through Confucius Institutes, practical skills through Luban Workshops — reflects a deliberate strategy to fuse investment with education and infrastructure with human capital.
As the students in Tashkent making mooncakes and the robotics trainees in Astana show, the Belt and Road is not only about connectivity between ports and pipelines. It is also about the quiet, daily work of building bridges between people — and the skills that will let them cross those bridges on their own.

articles.title: Kazakhstan Proposes Asian Transport Strategy at Baku Summit - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Kazakhstan Proposes Asian Transport Strategy at Baku Summit  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan has proposed a common transport strategy for Asia at a summit in Baku, where Central Asian leaders called for closer economic and technological cooperation.
The leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan presented their initiatives on October 15 at the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA). The proposals came amid negotiations to transform the forum into a full-fledged international organization.
CICA has particular historical significance for Kazakhstan. The idea of establishing the forum was first proposed in 1992 by Nursultan Nazarbayev, then the country’s president, at the United Nations General Assembly.
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for the development of a CICA Transport Connectivity Strategy. It would examine the potential of China’s Belt and Road Initiative, the International North–South Transport Corridor, the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, and the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, a planned transport link through Armenia.
The Middle Corridor connects China and Central Asia with European markets through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey. The North–South Corridor focuses on freight transportation between Russia, the Caspian region, Iran, and India. For Central Asian countries, developing several routes simultaneously means having more export options and reducing dependence on individual transit routes.
Tokayev also linked the prospects for improved transport connectivity to better relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia. Opening transport links in the South Caucasus could expand shipping options between Asia and Europe, although the specific arrangements for operating new routes have yet to be agreed upon.
Another proposal from Kazakhstan is a CICA Water Partnership for joint research, technology exchange, and water conservation. Tokayev also raised the issue of protecting the Caspian Sea. For Central Asia, water management is closely linked to growing demand from agriculture and the energy sector, as well as the effects of climate change.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov focused on investment and industrial cooperation. He called on CICA member states to pursue more joint projects, invited investment in the Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory, and proposed developing cross-border digital infrastructure. The country is building the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway to expand its transit connections.
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev presented proposals on the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI), confidence-building, and climate cooperation. He proposed establishing a CICA expert platform to develop common recommendations and coordinate practical measures on AI. Tashkent is pursuing digitalization domestically and is interested in international standards and technological partnerships.
The summit adopted the Baku Declaration and admitted Laos as CICA’s 29th member. The transport proposals came a week after regional leaders agreed to prioritize East–West and North–South transport routes at an October 8 meeting in Avaza, Turkmenistan.

articles.title: U.S. Targets Central Asia's Energy and Critical Minerals in Major Trade Push - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com

articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet the foreign ministers of the Central Asian republics - Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan - in Samarkand, Uzbekistan on 19 October 2026. Rubio will be accompanied by a delegation of more than 100 U.S. companies. Washington has framed the agenda around economic connectivity, energy security, and shared regional priorities. The meeting should convert earlier political commitments into financed projects, while managing the region's balancing act between the U.S., Russia, and China. The choice of Samarkand is symbolic as it hosted the first C5+1 ministerial in 2015.
The C5+1 was launched in 2015 and organizes U.S. engagement with the five republics around three pillars: economics, energy, and security; the Critical Minerals Dialogue operates in parallel. The Central Asian foreign ministers visited Washington in November last year, where Rubio said he intended to visit the region in 2026. The size of the business delegation signals that Washington wants commercial results rather than another declaration and may be seeking to lock down its influence in the region which escalates the conflict with neighboring Iran.
The key issues
Critical minerals and processing. Central Asia holds significant deposits of tungsten, uranium, rare earths, copper, and other strategic minerals. The practical questions are which projects are bankable, who provides geological data and financing, and how much processing happens in the region rather than abroad. The republics want value-added production, not raw-ore exports, and Uzbekistan has said this explicitly, though the region’s water deficit may limit processing opportunity. Ministers should identify a short list of flagship projects with named partners and timelines and agree on transparent licensing and investor protections.
Connectivity and trade corridors. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route ("Middle Corridor") across the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, and Georgia, and onward to Europe via Turkey, offers an alternative to routes via Russia, but it is constrained by port capacity, rail interoperability, customs delays, and tariff stacking. Issues to address include harmonized customs procedures, digital trade documentation, financing for rolling stock and port upgrades, and coordination with Caucasus transit partners. Ministers need a concrete corridor roadmap, not general language on improving connectivity. Related: Europe’s Gas Prices Close to 2022 High as Hormuz LNG Flows Remain Limited
Energy security. Central Asia needs reliable power for its own growth and has export potential in hydropower, solar, wind, and natural gas. Priorities include grid integration and regional power trade, U.S. technology and investment in generation and storage, and nuclear and natural gas-related cooperation where relevant. Winter supply reliability and aging Soviet-era infrastructure remain acute vulnerabilities.
Water and climate resilience. Water is tied directly to energy: upstream states (Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan) want hydropower, while downstream states (Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan) need irrigation flows. Glacier melt and drought are intensifying the pressure. The U.S. should offer data, monitoring, and technical assistance, and can support regional frameworks without taking sides on specific dams or allocation disputes.
The region is in the midst of a water crisis and faces a “water debt” - a financing gap of over US$12?billion by 2030 to modernize water and sanitation infrastructure. A lack of water will endanger the region’s ambitious development plans and may become a source of political instability.
Investment climate and business follow-through. The American delegation will want clarity on regulatory predictability, contract enforcement, dispute resolution, currency convertibility, and favorable tax treatment. For Washington, financing tools such as the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and the Export-Import Bank of the United States are Washington key tools to secure deals. For Uzbekistan, World Trade Organization accession and improved trade access are priorities. Ministers should set up a mechanism, ideally a standing business council or working group, to track which announced deals actually close.
Security, Iran, Afghanistan, and counterterrorism. Security cooperation covers border management, counterterrorism, counter-narcotics, and information sharing. Afghanistan is the hardest question: the republics view the Taliban relationship pragmatically and are deepening trade, transit, and energy links with Kabul, while the U.S. wants to avoid steps that legitimize the Taliban. The republics actively trade with Iran and Trump’s threat to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic is causing anxiety in the region. A frank exchange on red lines, trade, projects such as transit and electricity lines, and shared threat assessments is a must.
Strategic balance and sanctions. The republics value the C5+1 as a way to diversify partnerships, not to choose sides as the region is newly independent and not part of someone else’s empire for the first time since the 18th Century. Russian and Chinese influence is deeply embedded through trade, labor migration, energy infrastructure, cultural, and security ties. Sanctions compliance, particularly re-export of restricted goods to Russia, is a sensitive issue that should be raised privately rather than publicly. Washington should present itself as offering options, not demanding alignment with its grievances with its superpower competitors.
Governance and civil society. The rule of law, judicial independence, media freedom, and civil society underpin long-term investor confidence. The Trump administration prioritizes commercial and security interests, but language on institutional reform tied to investment protection can address governance without public confrontation or the appearance of American meddling.
The path to success
The republics expect investment and market access; U.S. companies expect predictability. Both sides risk disappointment if announcements outpace deal closings. The five capitals work to present a united front, but they do not always agree. Turkmenistan is “permanently neutral” and is more cautious about regional frameworks.
Moscow and Beijing will watch the meeting closely. Tweeting about it as anti-Russian or anti-Chinese would complicate the republics’ positions. Washington should seek commitments on human rights improvements. Omitting governance entirely could draw criticism from the U.S. Congress and civil society, while pressing too hard (and publicly) could reduce regional goodwill.
Washington must be clear that it is a reliable, long-term, commercial and security partner that respects the sovereignty of each state and offers real alternatives, not conditions, and won’t press-gang the republics into its conflicts with China, Russia, Afghanistan, and Iran. The republics should stress that regional cooperation, especially on water, transit, and customs, multiplies the value of external investment and strengthens bargaining power with all partners.

The Chinese Ministry of Defense’s announcement of a “joint support and training center” at an airport in Ban Keun, Laos, on Sept. 29 drew attention to the People’s Liberation Army’s growing footprint in Southeast Asia. Although China does not call it a “base” and said it’s “not targeted at any third party,” it is China’s first publicly acknowledged overseas military facility centered on airpower. Ban Keun joins Djibouti and Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base as nodes in a burgeoning network of overseas Chinese security infrastructure.
Concern is understandable. While smaller than China’s base in Djibouti, satellite imagery reveals eight light attack aircraft and support vehicles on a 2,000-meter runway that is currently under construction. Although insufficient to support long-range bombers, the facility likely benefits China’s logistics and intelligence capabilities, diversifies Southeast Asian base access beyond Cambodia, and ties Laos into its arms sales network. The joint center could eventually enhance the People’s Liberation Army Air Force’s power projection across mainland Southeast Asia, potentially affecting U.S. forces operating in the eastern Indian Ocean. For Vietnam, this development deepens its sense of siege.
The reflex among many policymakers in Washington after each rumored or announced Chinese military facility overseas is to interpret it through the lens of U.S.-Chinese competition. In Cambodia’s case with Ream, Washington imposed sanctions as punishment. Yet, this reflex misunderstands the nuanced interests driving regional partners to work with China — and how to counter it.
While the aviation facility in Laos demonstrates Beijing’s growing security presence in Southeast Asia, alignment is driven by diverse threat perceptions, notably regime security and intra-ASEAN concerns, rather than U.S.-China Cold War dynamics. Regional governments continue to hedge, leaving an opening for the United States to compete effectively with Beijing.
Compared to U.S. regional security engagement, China’s presence is less extensive but growing. China continues to militarize South China Sea land features. In mainland Southeast Asia, the Laos airfield joins the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, which opened in 2025 — officially under Cambodian control — and houses a rotating naval deployment. Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand stand out for the depth of military-to-military relationships with Beijing, while Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand have recently established 2+2 dialogues with China, involving foreign and defense ministers from both countries. Arms sales are also a growth area for Beijing. Indonesia expects the delivery of J-10 fighter jets, while Beijing surpassed the United States as Bangkok’s primary supplier.
However, China’s strongest comparative advantage over the United States is its regime security provision. The Global Security Initiative, one of four foreign policy cooperation frameworks promoted by Beijing, promises internal security assistance to its authoritarian partners, boosting state capacity while advancing its preferred governance norms. Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar’s junta, and Vietnam have all formally signed on. Although Bangkok remains outside the framework, internal security and police cooperation (particularly targeting scam centers in Myanmar) mirror the Thai military’s warm relations with the People’s Liberation Army.
Given the Chinese Communist Party’s holistic security conception equating party rule with national security, internal security arrangements often bleed over into external military cooperation. Notably, Beijing upgraded its 2+2 security dialogues with Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam to 3+3 in 2026 by including the internal security ministries. For each of these regimes, China’s internal security provision is critical, as Beijing can export its substantial know-how in high-tech surveillance and paramilitary policing. In Vietnam’s case, the internal security cooperation addresses some of the paradox in its approach to China: despite threatening Vietnam’s South China Sea claims, China likely won’t overthrow the Communist Party of Vietnam, but a revolution could.
Viewed through the lens of U.S.-Chinese competition, one could assume that China’s growing security presence in Southeast Asia comes at Washington’s expense. The United States is distracted and underinvested in Southeast Asia, and China’s deepening security ties augment its unassailable economic predominance. Singaporean think tank ISEAS’ annual survey of ASEAN elites found in 2026 that a majority would side with Beijing if forced to make a choice in alignment.
Yet, the geopolitical landscape in Southeast Asia remains in flux, and alignments are multifaceted and ultimately transitory due to the region’s complex web of threat perceptions, including vis-à-vis China. Indeed, ISEAS’ 2025 survey found that a majority would side with the United States — perhaps due to renewed South China Sea tensions. In 2024, China led at 50.5 percent after a U.S. lead in prior years, likely as a result of U.S. support for Israel. Rather than representing durable shifts in regional alignment, the survey instead reflects in-the-moment reactions to specific events. Indeed, diving into other areas of the survey, such as which geopolitical events rank as top concerns for ASEAN governments, one finds little consensus on the perceived threats that drive alignment.
The region’s diverse and shifting threat perceptions, not great-power competition, do more to explain the incentives to forge closer security ties to China. Despite the bloc’s self-proclaimed role in reducing state-to-state conflict since the Cold War, some ASEAN states fear each other more than China or the United States, while also seeing Beijing as a friend in some respects (internal security) and a foe in others (maritime disputes). Southeast Asian governments do not evaluate China and the United States solely through the lens of great-power competition. Instead, their behavior reflects shifting calculations of external threat, internal regime security, and intraregional rivalries.
Landlocked Laos, as a fellow communist government, seems a natural partner for China, as it does not see Beijing as a direct security threat. Air force training and support boost Laos’ own capabilities, while ensuring Chinese economic assistance, despite the clear risks of dependence. If it can position itself as China’s preferred client, then it stands to benefit.
Although often derided in Washington as a “Chinese puppet state,” Cambodia’s regional security environment is more dangerous than Laos’. In addition to regime security considerations, part of the strategic calculus driving outreach to Beijing is to hedge against the potential security threats from its neighbors, Vietnam and Thailand. In 2025, disputes over land along their border sparked a short but sharp armed conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, which ended in a fragile ceasefire. Still-simmering Thai-Cambodian tensions underscore the risk of renewed war, incentivizing Phnom Penh to hope that security ties to China can offset relative weakness vis-à-vis its historic rivals or, at the very least, keep Beijing engaged as a friendly mediator.
This impulse — along with distrust of complete dependence upon Beijing — has spurred Phnom Penh to renew ties with the United States under the Trump administration, which is less concerned about human rights than past U.S. presidencies. After a 10-year hiatus, Washington and Phnom Penh plan to relaunch joint military exercises in 2027. Cambodia welcomed a U.S. Navy visit to Ream Naval Base earlier this year, presenting the base as under its control, not China’s. Simultaneously, Cambodia continues to pursue security ties with other powers, notably Japan.
Despite Thai elites seeing China as the preferred partner, Thailand is in a similarly complex position. That Chinese weapons in Cambodian hands ended up deployed on the battlefield became a sore point. In some cases, China’s behavior has generated concerns about its political influence. During a 2025 joint crackdown on scam centers, a senior Chinese official personally oversaw the repatriation of Chinese detainees from Myanmar through Thailand, prompting debate about the extent of China’s involvement in sensitive security and law enforcement matters on Thai territory along the Myanmar border. The official later apologized for the “misunderstanding” of China’s rapid actions that generated the perception it does not respect Thai sovereignty. Importantly, Thailand has not jettisoned its defense ties with the United States, even if the alliance is weaker than in past decades. U.S.-Thai military exercise Cobra Gold remains the largest in Southeast Asia, and the two sides have expressed the intent to sign a new joint vision statement by the end of 2026.
Vietnam, meanwhile, demonstrates that analysis predicated on external security alone misses a key element: regime security. Vietnam, as Laos’ closest partner, will not rest easy with the announcement of a People’s Liberation Army Air Force presence to its west. Hemmed in by China’s island-building in the South China Sea and Beijing’s close ties to Cambodia, Hanoi is deeply concerned, having fought a war with its northern neighbor in 1979 and clashed at sea since. That security anxiety drives the U.S.-Vietnam rapprochement of recent decades and keeps Vietnam close to Russia.
Yet, in a reminder that few relationships within ASEAN are one-dimensional, Vietnamese-Lao bilateral ties have seemingly suffered little or no damage over the air force facility, while Hanoi’s Communist Party-to-Party relations with Beijing have deepened in recent years. China and North Korea have officially opened the New Yalu River Bridge, also called the Amnok River bridge, China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reports.
In a video address at the opening ceremony on Thursday, China’s Premier Li Qiang said relations between the two countries “are entering a new stage and opening a new chapter”, Xinhua reported.
Li said the cross-border infrastructure project was championed by Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Li said the bridge’s opening will strongly promote bilateral economic and trade cooperation while also further strengthening people-to-people exchanges and the emotional bonds between the two countries.
At the opening ceremony, Pak Thae Song, the premier of the North Korean cabinet said the bridge would accelerate the prosperity of the two countries and the well-being of both populations, adding new momentum to a mutually beneficial economic cooperation, North Korea’s state media KCNA said on Friday.
According to KCNA, Pak Thae Song emphasized North Korea’s consistent stance towards advancing North Korea-China relations.
China completed its side of the bridge in 2014, hoping to boost trade ties. However, North Korea left its side unfinished for years as relations soured after Beijing supported United Nations sanctions over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests.
The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea opened earlier this month.
China-North Korea relations
China’s exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3bn last year, 25 percent up from the previous year. Xi was welcomed in Pyongyang in June for the first time since 2019.
Since 2018, Beijing has tried to repair ties with Pyongyang, which also briefly began improving relations with Washington around the same time.
The China-North Korea relationship was forged during the Korean War. In 1961, the two countries signed the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which remains China’s only formal military alliance.
The treaty contains a mutual defence clause committing either side to assist the other if one comes under armed attack.
Although China was North Korea’s main diplomatic partner and protector for decades, relations strained after Beijing in 2017 supported tightening sanctions on Pyongyang for its nuclear weapons programme.
Analysts say North Korea’s recent growing relationship with Russia may have changed the balance of Pyongyang’s diplomatic dependence, reducing its reliance on Beijing.
North Korea and Russia signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in 2024, including a mutual defence provision. Military and political ties between the two countries have grown considerably stronger, with North Korea deploying thousands of troops to fight in Russia’s war on Ukraine.
United States President Donald Trump also signalled interest in repairing relations with Pyongyang last month, after his talks with Kim abruptly ended in 2019. In his second term, Trump has floated meeting Kim again, though no official meeting has been set.
North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, exchanges with China could involve goods North Korea needs to develop its civilian economy, according to analysts.

During talks in Tbilisi, Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan and Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze agreed to promote cooperation in trade, investment, tourism, aviation, and education, aiming to develop bilateral relations in a substantive and effective manner.
During her official visit to Georgia, on the afternoon of October 12, 2026, in the capital Tbilisi, Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan held talks with the host country's Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.
Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze welcomed Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan and the Vietnamese delegation on their official visit to Georgia; expressing confidence that the visit would be an important impetus to further promote the traditional friendship between Vietnam and Georgia in all fields.
The Georgian Prime Minister expressed his pleasure and appreciation for the achievements in bilateral cooperation over the past period, especially in the fields of politics , diplomacy, economics, trade, investment, and tourism.
Congratulating Vietnam on its socio-economic development achievements in recent years, the Georgian Prime Minister stated that Georgia's GDP is also projected to grow by more than 9% in 2025. He emphasized that Georgia highly values its relationship with Vietnam, noting the many similarities and complementary strengths between the two countries. Georgia's unique geographical location between the two continents of Asia and Europe makes it a key player in connectivity and transit, and it is investing heavily in railway and maritime infrastructure. He expressed a desire for further strengthening of these connections between the two countries. He noted that bilateral trade has increased sixfold over the past five years, and that the Georgian government is striving to create a healthy and attractive investment environment, hoping to attract more Vietnamese businesses to invest in Georgia.
Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze stated that tourism cooperation has grown quite strongly, with the number of Vietnamese tourists visiting Georgia increasing by 41% in the first six months of 2026 alone. He expressed hope that the two countries would soon open direct flights, further promoting bilateral cooperation and making Georgia an increasingly preferred destination for Vietnamese tourists. Georgia also has many prestigious and long-established universities that have previously accepted many Vietnamese students, which is another area with great potential for cooperation between the two sides.
Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan thanked the Government and people of Georgia for the warm and cordial welcome extended to the delegation; affirming that Vietnam values the traditional friendship with Georgia and wishes to work with Georgia to further deepen, strengthen, and enhance the effectiveness of bilateral relations.

The Vice President congratulated Georgia on its achievements in recent years; suggested that both sides promote bilateral exchange and contact mechanisms; strengthen exchanges of delegations at all levels and through all channels; coordinate in reviewing and improving the legal framework to create favorable conditions for cooperation in areas where both sides have strengths and needs; requested Georgia to create more favorable conditions for Vietnamese goods to access the Georgian market; and encouraged businesses from both countries to explore cooperation opportunities in areas where they have strengths and complement each other.
At the same time, we should focus on promoting cooperation in areas where both countries have great potential, such as tourism, culture, education and training, especially in areas where Vietnam has extensive experience, such as agriculture, agricultural product processing, infrastructure development, and innovation; promoting air connectivity and further facilitating people-to-people exchanges, cultural exchanges, and culinary exchanges to enhance contact and mutual understanding between the people of the two countries.
Both sides agreed that Vietnam-Georgia relations are facing many new development opportunities and need to be promoted in a substantive and effective manner, in line with the interests and potential of each country; both sides will continue to coordinate and support each other in multilateral organizations and forums, especially the United Nations and regional cooperation mechanisms; and strengthen cooperation in the fields of defense and security, especially in addressing non-traditional security challenges...
“Vietnam is ready to act as a bridge to promote cooperation between Georgia and Vietnam and ASEAN countries; welcomes Georgia’s strengthening of relations with ASEAN and Southeast Asian countries; and proposes that the two sides coordinate to promote connectivity between the two economies, leveraging each country’s advantages to expand markets, connect businesses, and promote inter-regional cooperation projects,” Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan affirmed.
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze affirmed his desire to promote comprehensive relations with Vietnam and ASEAN countries, and expressed his readiness to act as a bridge to promote relations between Vietnam and countries in Central Asia, the Caucasus, and Europe.
Welcoming the signing of cooperation documents by agencies of the two countries within the framework of the visit, Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze affirmed that these are practical steps to create a favorable framework to promote and further expand cooperation between the two countries.
You may also like
During the visit, the Vietnamese Ministry of Foreign Affairs signed a Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation with the Georgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs; the Vietnamese Ministry of Agriculture and Environment signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Georgian Ministry of Environment and Agriculture on cooperation in the agricultural sector.
The two leaders agreed to instruct the ministries and agencies of both countries to urgently exchange information, quickly finalize and sign other important documents to promote trade, investment, tourism, and people-to-people exchanges, such as an agreement on investment promotion and protection, an agreement on avoiding double taxation, and an agreement on visa exemption for holders of diplomatic and official passports…
On this occasion, Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan suggested that the agencies of the two countries coordinate closely and implement meaningful activities to commemorate the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 2027, and expressed her hope to welcome Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze to visit Vietnam on this occasion.
The Georgian Prime Minister expressed his gratitude and his desire to visit Vietnam soon to further discuss ways and measures to promote all-round relations between the two countries.
